title: Composite Pattern
tagline: Model part-whole hierarchies so clients can treat individual objects and collections of objects through a single uniform interface.

sections.content:
**The core problem looks like this:** you are building a file-system browser. A `File` has a `getSize()` method that returns its own size in bytes. A `Folder` also needs a `getSize()` method — but its size is the sum of everything inside it, including nested folders. Without any pattern, your calling code has to write:

```js
if (item instanceof Folder) { /* recursive sum */ } else { /* scalar */ }
```

Every place in the codebase that touches the tree must repeat this conditional. Add a new node type — say `Symlink` or `Archive` — and every one of those sites must be updated. The code is **open to breakage and closed to extension**, the exact opposite of the Open/Closed Principle.

**The Composite pattern** cuts through this by giving both `File` (a *leaf*) and `Folder` (a *composite*) the same interface: `FileSystemItem`. The `Folder`'s `getSize()` simply calls `getSize()` on each of its children and sums the results. If a child is itself a `Folder`, that call recurses. If a child is a `File`, it returns a scalar. The recursion terminates naturally — no explicit type-checking required, anywhere.

The client calls `root.getSize()` and gets the correct total for an arbitrarily deep tree, with zero `instanceof` checks. That is the promise of Composite.

**Where you already see this every day:** the HTML DOM (every `Element` can contain other `Element`s — `appendChild`, `querySelector`, `innerHTML` all work uniformly on any element regardless of depth), React component trees (a component can render other components to any depth), file systems, GUI toolkits, organisation charts, menu hierarchies, bill-of-materials in manufacturing, and expression trees in compilers and query builders.

sections.title: An Organisation Chart Where Every Node Has a Payroll Cost
sections.content:
Picture a company's organisational chart. At the bottom are individual contributors (ICs): each has a salary. Above them are team leads, who have their own salary but also manage some ICs. Above them are VPs, each managing multiple teams. At the top is the CEO.

Now ask: **what is the total payroll cost of the Engineering organisation?** You want to call `engineering.getTotalCost()` and get the right answer without caring whether `engineering` is a single person or an 800-person department.

If an individual contributor's `getTotalCost()` returns their own salary, and a department's `getTotalCost()` returns the sum of `getTotalCost()` across all its direct reports — you have Composite. The calculation cascades through the tree automatically. Add a new contractor node type: as long as it implements `getTotalCost()`, every department above it gets the correct roll-up with no changes to existing code.

This is the fundamental insight: **treat the individual and the group identically through a shared operation, and let the tree structure handle the aggregation**.

sections.title: The Four Participants in Detail
sections.content:
**1. Component Interface** — the contract that both leaves and composites must fulfill. It declares every operation the client will ever call: `getSize()`, `print(indent)`, `getName()`. Some designs put `add()` and `remove()` here too (see the Transparency vs. Safety section below). The client only ever holds a reference typed as `Component` — it never knows whether it has a leaf or a composite in hand.

**2. Leaf** — a primitive node with no children. It implements the Component Interface with concrete, scalar behaviour. A `File` knows its own size directly; it does not delegate. Leaf nodes are where the actual data or computation lives. Implementations are straightforward — no iteration, no recursion.

**3. Composite** — a container node. It stores a collection of children (each typed as `Component`, so each child can be a Leaf or another Composite). Its `operation()` is the key: it iterates over children, calls `operation()` on each, and aggregates the results. In `getSize()` that aggregation is a sum; in `print()` it is sequential calls with increasing indentation; in `validate()` it might be a logical AND of all children's validity.

**4. Client** — the code that uses the tree. It calls methods on a root `Component` and never inspects whether it is a Leaf or a Composite. The client code is **closed for modification** even as the tree grows more complex or new node types are added.

The power emerges from the recursive structure: a Composite's children list contains Components, not specifically Leaves. So children may themselves be Composites, which may contain further Composites. The tree can be arbitrarily deep, and every level of `operation()` delegation works the same way.

sections.title: Transparency vs. Safety: Where to Put add() and remove()
sections.content:
This is the central design tension in the Composite pattern, and the GoF book discusses it explicitly.

**Transparent approach** — put `add()`, `remove()`, and `getChildren()` on the Component interface. Every node, leaf or composite, exposes the same full interface. The client can call `add()` on any node without casting. The downside: a Leaf has to implement `add()` and `remove()` — it either throws `UnsupportedOperationException` (Java) or does nothing, which is semantically weird. The API lies about what a Leaf can do.

**Safe approach** — put `add()`, `remove()`, and `getChildren()` only on Composite. Leaves do not have these methods, so the type system prevents callers from accidentally calling `add()` on a Leaf. The downside: when building the tree, the client must either use the concrete `Composite` type (losing interface uniformity) or downcast from `Component` to `Composite` — which is exactly the kind of type inspection the pattern is trying to eliminate.

**The practical resolution:** most real-world codebases use the safe approach for the runtime client code (which never needs to call `add()` — it just traverses and calls operations) but use concrete `Composite` types at tree-construction time. Tree construction is a one-time, structural concern; the runtime operations are where uniformity matters most.

In TypeScript and statically-typed languages, the safe approach gives compile-time guarantees. In JavaScript, the distinction is more stylistic — duck-typing means a client can call `add()` on anything and find out at runtime.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: Three things to notice: (1) `File.getSize()` returns a scalar — no delegation. (2) `Folder.getSize()` returns `reduce(...child.getSize()...)` — one line, fully recursive. (3) Adding the `Archive` leaf type required zero changes to `Folder`, `File`, or client code. The Open/Closed Principle is satisfied.

sections.title: TypeScript: Enforcing the Contract at Compile Time
sections.content:
JavaScript's dynamic typing makes the Composite pattern work but gives no safety net. TypeScript lets us express the interface explicitly and get compile-time guarantees.

The key is an **interface or abstract class** that both `Leaf` and `Composite` implement. For the safe variant, `add()` and `remove()` live only on the `Composite` class, not on the interface. The client receives a `Component` — it can call `operation()` but not `add()`. Only tree-building code needs to reference `Composite` directly.

For the transparent variant, you can add `add()` and `remove()` to the interface with optional/default implementations: in TypeScript abstract classes, the leaf subclass simply omits an override of `add()` (which throws by default). TypeScript will flag any leaf that accidentally tries to receive children.

TypeScript also enables the **Visitor pattern** variant of Composite traversal (using discriminated unions), but that is a separate pattern. For Composite, the interface approach is idiomatic.

**Generic Composite** is another TypeScript power move: `Composite<T extends Component<V>, V>` lets you build type-safe trees where the operation result type `V` is parameterised. A `getSize()` tree returns `number`; a `validate()` tree returns `boolean`; a `render()` tree returns `VNode`. The structure is reusable across all of them.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The `measureTree` function accepts a `UIComponent` — it works identically on a `Button` leaf and a `Panel` composite. The TypeScript compiler enforces that only `Panel` has `add()` — a client holding a `UIComponent` reference cannot accidentally call `add()` on a `Button`.

sections.title: Recursive Traversal Patterns: More Than Just Summation
sections.content:
Summation (`getSize()`, `getRenderTime()`) is the introductory example, but the Composite pattern supports any recursive operation. Here are the traversal patterns you will encounter:

**Accumulate** — collect all matching nodes. Example: `findAll(predicate)` on a DOM-like tree. The composite iterates children, collects their results, and flattens them into one array. Each leaf either includes itself or returns `[]`.

**Reduce/Fold** — combine all leaf values with a combining function. This generalises summation: use the same structure with `Math.max` instead of `+` and you get a `getMaxDepth()` operation.

**Validate** — return `true` only if every node in the tree satisfies a condition. The composite returns `children.every(c => c.validate())`. Short-circuits on the first failure. Used in form libraries where a form group's validity is the AND of all its field validities.

**Render/Serialize** — turn the tree into a string or DOM node. The composite wraps its children's rendered output in a container tag. HTML `innerHTML` works this way.

**Visitor** — separate the traversal algorithm from the nodes themselves. Each node accepts a visitor object; the visitor defines what to do at each node type. This extends the Composite pattern without modifying node classes — useful when you need many different operations on the same tree structure.

**Count** — `count()` where composite returns `children.reduce((n, c) => n + c.count(), 0)` and leaf returns 1. Gives the total number of leaf nodes in the tree.

**Depth** — `getDepth()` where leaf returns 0 and composite returns `1 + Math.max(...children.map(c => c.getDepth()))`. Finds the deepest path.

All of these follow the same structural template: the composite asks each child for its answer and combines the answers. The template never changes — only the combining step changes.

sections.title: Real-World Frameworks That Use Composite
sections.content:
Understanding the Composite pattern unlocks a lot of framework internals:

**HTML DOM** — The canonical real-world example. `HTMLElement` implements `EventTarget` and `Node`. Every element can contain child elements. `querySelectorAll`, `addEventListener`, `innerHTML`, `getBoundingClientRect` (which aggregates child boxes) — all work identically on a single `<span>` and on a `<div>` containing 10,000 children. The DOM is a Composite tree.

**React component tree** — A `React.Component` renders JSX that may contain other components. React's reconciler traverses this tree recursively during render, diff, and commit phases. The Fiber architecture is essentially a linked-list representation of a Composite tree. `React.Children.map` and `React.Children.count` are explicit Composite traversal utilities.

**Java Swing / AWT** — `Container extends Component`. Every Swing widget is a `Component`. Containers (JPanel, JFrame, JScrollPane) implement `add(Component c)` — the textbook safe Composite. Layout managers traverse the component tree to compute sizes and positions.

**Apache POI (Excel/Word documents)** — A `Workbook` contains `Sheet`s, which contain `Row`s, which contain `Cell`s. Operations like applying a style or computing column widths walk this tree using Composite delegation.

**GNU Make / Gradle dependency graphs** — Build tasks form a directed acyclic graph where each task's `execute()` first executes its dependencies. This is a Composite with shared nodes (a DAG rather than a pure tree), but the recursive delegation pattern is the same.

**Expression trees in ORMs and query builders** — A SQL `WHERE` clause like `(age > 18 AND country = 'US') OR vip = true` is represented as a tree of `Predicate` objects. `AndPredicate` and `OrPredicate` are composites; `FieldPredicate` is a leaf. Calling `predicate.toSQL()` recursively serialises the tree.

**Three.js scene graph** — `Object3D` is both leaf (Mesh, Light) and composite (Group, Scene). The render loop calls `update()` on the scene root and the transform matrices propagate down through every child, grandchild, etc.

sections.title: Common Misconceptions and Edge Cases
sections.content:
**Misconception: Composite is just recursion.** Recursion is the mechanism, but the pattern is about the *design intent*: uniform treatment of leaf and composite through a shared interface. Plain recursion with `instanceof` checks is NOT the Composite pattern — it is exactly what the pattern replaces.

**Misconception: You must have a deep tree to benefit.** Even a two-level tree (items inside a group) benefits from Composite if you ever need to treat items and groups the same way.

**Circular references** — a Composite that contains itself (directly or indirectly) will cause infinite recursion. The pattern assumes a **strict tree** (acyclic). If you need shared nodes, you have a DAG and must track visited nodes during traversal (e.g., a Set of visited nodes) to prevent loops.

**Ordering matters for some operations** — `print(indent)` depends on child order; `getSize()` does not. When building a tree, ensure children are added in the correct semantic order if your operation is order-sensitive.

**Leaf `add()` in the transparent approach** — the idiomatic handling is to throw a clear error: `throw new Error('Cannot add children to a leaf node')`. This is better than silently ignoring the call, because silent failures hide bugs.

**Performance on very large trees** — recursive delegation creates one stack frame per level. For trees dozens of levels deep with millions of nodes, an iterative traversal using an explicit stack may be more memory-efficient. This is an optimisation concern, not a correctness concern.

**Caching aggregated results** — if the tree is large and `getSize()` is called frequently, consider caching the computed value and invalidating on `add()` or `remove()`. This is the Flyweight/Memo optimisation layered on top of Composite.

sections.content: **Origin:** The Composite pattern was documented in the GoF book (Design Patterns, 1994) using GUI widget hierarchies as the primary example. The book explicitly discusses the transparency vs. safety trade-off and recommends the transparent approach for maximum uniformity — though modern statically-typed languages tend to prefer the safe approach for its compile-time guarantees. The GoF also notes that Composite and Decorator are often used together: Decorator wraps a single Component (adding responsibilities), while Composite aggregates multiple Components. Both share the same Component interface, so a decorated component can live inside a composite transparently.

**When to use Composite:**
- You have a tree structure where nodes can be either primitives or containers of other nodes.
- You want client code to treat a single object and a collection of objects identically.
- Adding new node types should not require changing existing traversal code.
- The operation on a composite is a well-defined aggregation of the same operation on its children.

**When NOT to use Composite:**
- Your structure is flat or has a fixed, known number of levels — the pattern adds unnecessary abstraction.
- Leaf and composite operations are radically different — forcing a shared interface produces awkward no-op methods on leaves.
- You need to distinguish leaf from composite frequently at runtime for non-traversal reasons — the pattern's value comes from NOT needing to distinguish.
- Performance is critical and the tree is extremely large — consider caching or iterative traversal instead of pure recursion.

**Frequently confused with:** Iterator (which traverses a collection but does not imply part-whole hierarchy), Decorator (which wraps a single object, not a collection), and simple polymorphism (which handles type variation but not recursive aggregation).

items: The **Composite pattern** lets clients treat leaf nodes and composite nodes identically through a shared Component interface — eliminating `instanceof` checks from traversal code entirely.

**Recursive delegation** is the engine: a composite's `operation()` calls `operation()` on each child and aggregates. Leaves return scalars; composites aggregate. The recursion terminates naturally at every leaf.

The pattern satisfies the **Open/Closed Principle**: adding a new node type (a new leaf class) requires no changes to existing composites, other leaves, or client code — just implement the Component interface.

The **transparency vs. safety trade-off** (putting `add()`/`remove()` on the Component interface vs. only on Composite) determines whether the client has full interface uniformity or compile-time type safety when building trees.

**Any aggregation operation** works with the pattern — summation, validation (AND of children), rendering (wrap in container), collection (flatten children results), depth calculation (1 + max of children depths). The structure is the same; only the combining step changes.

The **HTML DOM, React component trees, Java Swing, Three.js scene graphs, and ORM expression trees** are all real-world Composite implementations — understanding the pattern explains why they behave the way they do.

**Watch out for:** circular references (infinite recursion), performance on extremely large trees (consider caching aggregated results), and the misuse of the transparent approach producing no-op leaf methods that hide bugs rather than failing loudly.

quiz.question: What is the central problem the Composite pattern is designed to solve?
options: Converting an object's interface to match what a client expects
Eliminating instanceof checks so clients treat leaf nodes and composite nodes through a single uniform interface
Deferring the creation of expensive objects until they are needed
Notifying multiple observers when an object's state changes
quiz.explanation: The Composite pattern's core purpose is uniform treatment: both a single File (leaf) and a Folder containing thousands of files (composite) respond to the same getSize() call without the client needing to distinguish between them.

quiz.question: In the Composite pattern, which participant stores a list of children and delegates operation() to each of them?
options: Leaf — because it handles the actual data
Component Interface — because it defines the shared contract
Client — because it initiates the traversal
Composite — because it is the container node that aggregates children
quiz.explanation: The Composite node holds a children list typed as Component[]. Its operation() iterates that list, calls operation() on each child, and aggregates. Leaves return scalars; the Client fires one call on the root.

quiz.question: A Folder's getSize() is implemented as: `return this._children.reduce((sum, c) => sum + c.getSize(), 0)`. What happens when a child is itself a Folder?
options: It throws an error because a Folder cannot call getSize() on another Folder
It calls the same getSize() recursively on that Folder, which in turn sums its own children
It returns 0 for that child because Folders have no direct size
The outer Folder must handle this case with an instanceof check
quiz.explanation: Because both File and Folder implement the same interface, `c.getSize()` is a polymorphic call. When c is a Folder, the Folder's getSize() executes — which recursively sums its own children. No instanceof check needed; the recursion terminates at leaf Files.

quiz.question: What is the 'transparency vs. safety' trade-off in the Composite pattern?
options: Whether the tree stores nodes by value or by reference
Whether to use synchronous or asynchronous traversal

Whether add() and remove() live on the Component interface (transparent, full uniformity, but leaf must handle them) or only on Composite (safe, type-enforced, but requires casting when building the tree)
Whether the pattern uses inheritance or composition internally
quiz.explanation: If add()/remove() are on the Component interface, every node looks the same (transparent) but Leaf must implement or reject child-management methods. If they are only on Composite, the type system prevents adding children to a Leaf, but tree-building code must reference Composite concretely.

quiz.question: You add a new `Archive` class that implements `FileSystemItem` and returns the sum of its compressed entries from getSize(). How many existing classes (File, Folder, and client code) need to change?
options: All three — File, Folder, and client must register the new type
Only Folder — it must add a case for Archive in its getSize() logic
Zero — Archive just implements the interface; existing code delegates polymorphically
Only the client — it must cast to Archive when computing size
quiz.explanation: This is the Open/Closed Principle in action. Folder.getSize() calls child.getSize() on each Component. Archive implements getSize() — so Folder's reduce() works without modification. Client code calls root.getSize() unchanged. No existing code changes.

quiz.question: Which of the following is NOT a valid operation pattern for the Composite pattern?
options: validate() — composite returns children.every(c => c.validate())
count() — composite returns children.reduce((n, c) => n + c.count(), 0); leaf returns 1
update() — composite subscribes all children to an event stream independently
getDepth() — composite returns 1 + Math.max(...children.map(c => c.getDepth())); leaf returns 0
quiz.explanation: Subscribing children to an independent event stream is the Observer pattern, not Composite. Composite operations must aggregate child results in a well-defined way. validate(), count(), and getDepth() all follow the canonical template: composite aggregates, leaf returns a scalar.

quiz.question: The HTML DOM's querySelectorAll('.btn') works the same on a single <span> and on a <div> containing 5000 children. What design pattern does this illustrate?
options: Singleton — because there is only one document
Composite — every Element implements the same interface whether it has 0 or N children
Template Method — querySelector defines a skeleton algorithm
Facade — querySelector hides the complexity of tree traversal
quiz.explanation: Every DOM Element implements the same interface (querySelector, appendChild, childNodes) regardless of how many children it has. This uniform treatment of both leaf-like elements and container elements is the hallmark of the Composite pattern.

quiz.question: A tree has a Folder at the root containing 3 Files (10 KB, 20 KB, 5 KB) and one inner Folder containing 2 Files (50 KB, 15 KB). What does root.getSize() return?
options: 35 KB
65 KB
100 KB
50 KB
quiz.explanation: Inner folder: 50 + 15 = 65 KB. Root: 10 + 20 + 5 + 65 = 100 KB. The composite delegates to the inner folder's getSize(), which itself recursively returns 65.

quiz.question: What is the primary risk of a circular reference (a Composite that indirectly contains itself) in the Composite pattern?
options: Compile-time error in all typed languages
Infinite recursion when calling any delegating operation like getSize()
The add() method silently ignores the circular reference
Memory leak but no runtime error
quiz.explanation: The Composite pattern assumes a strict tree (acyclic). If a Composite contains itself (directly or via chain), calling getSize() will recurse forever — each call delegates to children, one of which is the same node, causing a stack overflow. Prevention: validate on add() or track visited nodes during traversal.

quiz.question: Which scenario is the WORST fit for the Composite pattern?
options: A menu system where a MenuItem can be a simple action or a submenu containing more MenuItems
A bill-of-materials where an Assembly contains sub-assemblies and individual Parts
A flat configuration store where keys map directly to string values with no nesting
An expression tree where AND/OR nodes contain child predicates and leaf nodes are field comparisons
quiz.explanation: A flat key-value store has no part-whole hierarchy — there is nothing to compose, no tree to traverse. The Composite pattern adds abstraction overhead for zero gain here. The other three examples are all genuine tree hierarchies.
